verses.note: Fire and smoke are the signs of God's presence throughout the Old Testament. Abram sees, in a sleep of terror, a small form of what Israel will see at Sinai.

Joseph has the one opportunity of his life to impress Pharaoh, and he begins by denying his own ability and directing the king's attention to God. His later authority rests on that refusal to take the credit that belongs to God.

Moses asked to see God's glory (33:18) and was answered with a proclamation of God's goodness and name. In this chapter God's glory is revealed chiefly as his character, heard more than seen, which is the pattern John's Gospel follows when it speaks of glory ‘full of grace and truth’ (John 1:14).

God's glory changes the one who is near it. Moses reflects light he does not generate and does not notice, a picture the New Testament takes up for the transformation of believers who behold the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:18) and sees fulfilled in the transfigured Christ (Matthew 17:2).
The glory of the LORD that left the temple in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 10:18-19) returns, and this time all flesh sees it. John's Gospel says of the incarnate Word that we saw his glory (John 1:14).

Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave the temple before its fall (Ezekiel 10:18-19, 11:23) and return to a renewed temple (43:1-5). Isaiah's watchmen see that return. The exile's deepest loss was God's absence; its deepest comfort is his coming back.

God's concern for his name is not vanity; his name is his revealed character, and the nations' knowledge of the true God depends on it. Isaiah 48:9-11 and Psalm 106:8 make the same point. Because God's glory is the motive, his grace rests on something steadier than the recipients' worth.
God's saving intervention is described with the imagery of Sinai and the storm. The one who gave the covenant in thunder is the one who comes to defend the covenant people.

The glory seen on the mountain is not given to Jesus from outside, as light reflected on Moses' face, but shown from within. The church has read the transfiguration as a brief unveiling of the divine glory the Son always had, the glory John says the disciples beheld (John 1:14).

The glory that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) appears over a field near Bethlehem. Luke puts the presence of God's glory at the birth, a glory John will say was seen in the Word made flesh (John 1:14).

Glory, God's visible weight and splendor, was seen in the tabernacle cloud. Here it is seen in a person, and the Gospel will show it chiefly at the cross, where Jesus says the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified (12:23).

Glory is revealed at a small family feast, seen by servants and a few disciples, not by the crowd. John defines divine glory by what it does here: it supplies a need generously and quietly. The same pattern of hidden glory will reach its height at the cross.

In John, being glorified is not escape from the cross but the cross itself as the place where God's glory is shown, completed in resurrection and return to the Father. The Spirit flows from that glory.

The Son's glory is given, not seized. Jesus will pray for the Father to glorify him with the glory he had before the world existed (17:5), and that request, like this verse, shows the Son receiving honor from the Father rather than taking it.

God's glory is his own revealed majesty, and human beings were made to reflect it. Exchanging it for images is the reverse of the human vocation, which is why Paul later says all have sinned and lack God's glory (3:23) and that believers are being restored to it (8:29-30).

The glory humanity lacks is God's own, shared with his image-bearers. Paul's hope is its restoration: believers rejoice in hope of the glory of God (5:2) and are being transformed from glory to glory (2 Corinthians 3:18).
The glory of God is the believer's destiny, not only God's possession. Paul will say that those God justified he also glorified (8:30), as if the future were already done.
God's purpose in all his dealings, patience and wrath included, is to make known the riches of his glory to those who receive mercy. The glory prepared for them is the glory of 8:18 and 8:30.
The body sown in dishonor, whether in burial or in the humiliations of aging and illness, is raised in glory. Glory is not reserved for the soul; the body shares in it.
The cherubim ‘of glory’ marked the place where God's glory dwelt among his people (Exodus 25:22). The New Testament locates that glory in the Son (John 1:14, Hebrews 1:3).
